title: The Apache Wars
summary: Josh and Chuck, in honor of Native American Heritage Month, cover the Apache Wars, a long series of conflicts between the United States (and Mexico) and the Chiricahua Apache and related bands in the 1860s through 1886. They explain that "Apache" is a loose grouping of bands rather than one nation, describe Chiricahua society and the raiding economy, and walk through key events: the 1861 Bascom Affair over kidnapped Felix Ward, the 1863 killing of Mangas Coloradas, the 1871 Camp Grant Massacre and the 1872-1876 peace under Cochise, the renewed war under Geronimo, Victorio and Lozen, General George Crook's campaigns and Geronimo's repeated surrenders and escapes, General Nelson Miles's final pursuit, and Geronimo's exile and death at Fort Sill in Oklahoma. The episode closes with a listener mail segment and sign-off.

segments.title: Opening and introduction to the Apache Wars
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck frame the episode for Native American Heritage Month, call the Apache Wars the longest war the US has fought, and note that histories written by the victors painted the Apache with too broad a brush.

segments.title: Who the Apache were
segments.summary: The Apache are a loose group of related tribes, not one nation, who migrated from western Canada to the American Southwest. Their name likely came from the Zuni word for enemy. Bands were small, the Chiricahua were the central group, divided into four bands, and leadership, matrilineal marriage ties and internal disagreements about dealing with Americans varied widely.

segments.title: Raiding, Mexico and the Gila River homeland
segments.summary: Raiding was an economic necessity rather than malice, distinct from revenge-driven battles. The Apache were hostile to Mexicans, and Mangas Coloradas wanted an alliance with Americans against Mexico. The Chiricahua's homeland south of the Gila River in Arizona was valuable, placing them in the path of westward expansion and the Civil War.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Short break before the next segment.

segments.title: The Bascom Affair of 1861
segments.summary: Lieutenant George Bascom, a young and inexperienced officer, accused Cochise's band of kidnapping Felix Ward. At a meeting, Bascom held Cochise, who escaped by cutting through a tent, leaving his family hostage. Cochise took hostages in a raid; the Mexican hostages were killed and the American hostages were held. After negotiations failed, both sides executed hostages, including Cochise's brother. Many histories cite this as the start of the Apache Wars.

segments.title: Death of Mangas Coloradas
segments.summary: In 1863 Mangas Coloradas was invited to peace talks, held and executed, his body mutilated and his head sent to a phrenologist in New York. This is seen by many as a key turning point that showed the Union Army could not be trusted in peace talks.

segments.title: Civil War, raids and the Camp Grant Massacre
segments.summary: Civil War troops in the Southwest drew Apache raiding. Apache retreated into the desert rather than fight outgunned. In 1871 Tucson residents massacred a peaceful Apache camp under Eskiminzin at Camp Grant, killing 144 mostly women and children and enslaving about 27 children. President Grant was furious and sent a peace delegation.

segments.title: Cochise's truce and the San Carlos reservation
segments.summary: Grant's delegation offered a truce if the Chiricahua moved to San Carlos, which was called Hell's Forty Acres. Cochise negotiated a separate reservation instead. The peace lasted about four years until Cochise died of stomach cancer and incidents including killings of white men eroded the truce, and the second Apache War began.

segments.title: Geronimo's rise and the Victorio war
segments.summary: Naiche's stuttering-restricted negotiations used Geronimo as proxy. Taza moved with a third of the Apache to San Carlos while two-thirds followed Geronimo. Geronimo's raid captured Chief Loco. Geronimo's nickname origin is unknown. Chief Victorio's band left Ojo Caliente and fought for two years, with Mexican and American forces pursuing them, until Victorio was killed by Mexican forces. Lozen, his sister, was a famed fighter and strategist.

segments.title: General Crook, Geronimo's surrenders and exile
segments.summary: General George Crook, called the Tan Wolf, tracked Geronimo, and after an encounter Geronimo agreed to surrender. Geronimo surrendered and escaped four times. President Cleveland ordered unconditional surrender, Crook resigned, and General Nelson Miles took over. Miles used threats against imprisoned families to force Geronimo's final surrender, and Geronimo was exiled. He later toured with Buffalo Bill, rode in Teddy Roosevelt's parade, and died at Fort Sill, Oklahoma, of pneumonia.

segments.title: Aftermath and legacy
segments.summary: The Chiricahua were split between Fort Sill, Oklahoma and the Mescalero reservation, with about two-thirds moving to southern Arizona. Return to ancestral lands was delayed twenty-seven years. Sherman reportedly said the US should fight Mexico to take Arizona back. The Chiricahua Apache tribe's website now describes them as peaceful.

segments.title: Listener mail from Sarah
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck read a listener email from Sarah in Georgetown, Texas, who is working through the back catalog and says she is listening to the episode about kleptomaniacs. They discuss sandwiching episodes.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck invite listeners to email the show and note the show's production credits.
